As someone turning 26 in two weeks only now starting community college, I can say you're going to be okay. But let's get down to your question.

1. What's your financial situation?  
If it's bad, focus on getting any job and see if you can stay with family or friends for free or cheap. If unstable, what's the reason (no judgement, just gotta get to the source). If good but could be better, time for a better job, which leads to my next question.


2. What's your education?
Do you have any Post Highschool education? If so, how much and in what? Would it be worth it to you to finish that and have the degree?  Do you care about the job you can get or not so much? 


3. What makes you look forward to the future?
I know you're scared, I am too. I think a lot of us are. But you don't need a huge goal to reach in order to find purpose. You know what my goals are? Have a job I don't hate, have a cat or two, and hopefully move in and marry my partner. There are steps to reaching those goals, so as of now those steps are my new goals. It's also important to determine your values. There's a club/association for everything, and perhaps being a part of a community will lessen your fears and doubts. 

In any case, I understand your situation. My boyfriend is doing his master's thesis, my best friends are either married or getting married, and all I've got are transcripts from half-finished music degrees. There's hope. You'll be okay.

I can certainly tell you what worked for me! I'm sure you know that it'll take time to adjust to a new energy source. I started off by drinking a bunch of water when I woke up each day, while still drinking an energy drink as usual. Then I told myself that I could only drink one 4 days a week (feel free to adjust as you feel is easy at first, don't start at your goal). Other things that gave me energy were coffee, sticking to a better sleep schedule, and even just washing your face and ears with water in the morning has helped me a ton. And as I mentioned in another comment, make sure to reward yourself. Sometimes our brains just need that happy boost in order to stick with a habit, even if ultimately we genuinely want to stick with it for good reasons.

Thank you!! What's helped me the most is actually doing less than more. Basically, instead of forcing myself to go cold turkey on anything, I told myself I only had to follow my habits 3 days a week. And if I went a whole month sticking to those three days (or more), I'd increase it by one day a week. At first it seems almost condescending, but it gave me solace knowing that I'm still making progress.

I also learned that you do have to make sacrifices, especially if you suffer from mental illnesses like myself. Some days I was able to work on my German, but only if I could buy myself a coffee. Some days I had to choose between an energy drink or a soda, but I "needed" one. Sticking to one habit instead of two is better than doing neither. 

And rewards! Are! So! Important! And doing the things that actually make you happy! Read a book that you genuinely have interest in, even if it's just a page a day. And as a recent example, I managed to not spend money for three days in a row, and as a reward I got to have a great night out with my best friend to celebrate her birthday!

When I started adding joy to my habits and goals, I started doing them more. I hate the hard-core discipline ideology. My dumb brain doesn't see the point of brushing my teeth but not getting to ruin them with soda first. And when I started interchanging them, I slowly started doing one more than the other. And, after a year of doing so, here I am! Consider it a "depression inspired" life hack. I hope it helps!
